stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: When engineers dismantled a 1920s railway trestle in Ohio, they expected its timber pilings, which had sat underwater for nearly a century, to be badly weakened. Core samples showed the pilings to be anything but ______: they kept almost all of their original load-bearing strength. The oxygen-poor mud around them had apparently kept decay-causing fungi from growing.
explanation: Start with what the evidence shows: the pilings kept almost all of their strength. The phrase "anything but" reverses the blank, so the blank has to mean the opposite of strong. "Degraded" fits. The pilings were anything but degraded, which is why the engineers' expectation of weakness turned out wrong.

A.why: You matched the blank to the evidence (the strength the pilings kept) and skipped the reversal. "Anything but durable" would mean the pilings were weak, which is the opposite of what the core samples showed.

C.why: The passage says the pilings sat underwater for nearly a century. Calling them "anything but submerged" denies a fact the text states outright.

D.why: The passage never mentions upgrades or modernization. The test results after the colon are about strength, so they give no support for a claim about modernizing.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Some seismologists have dismissed the faint tremors that sometimes come before large earthquakes as ______, little more than random background noise in the Earth's crust. A 2025 analysis of 300 earthquakes along the Chilean coast challenges this view. In the days before 70 percent of those earthquakes, the tremors followed a consistent pattern, which suggests they may carry real information about an approaching rupture.
explanation: The blank sits inside the view that the passage then knocks down. The phrase "little more than random background noise" restates it, so the blank has to mean something like unimportant. "Inconsequential" fits. The new analysis challenges that dismissal by showing the tremors may matter after all.

A.why: You took what the new evidence shows (the tremors may carry information) and put it into the dismissive view. That is the opposite of the view the passage describes. Nobody calls something "little more than random background noise" because it is predictive.

C.why: How often the tremors occur is beside the point. The dismissive view is about whether they mean anything, and "frequent" does not restate "little more than random background noise."

D.why: The passage calls the tremors faint. Dismissing them as destructive clashes with that description and with the idea that they are just noise.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Historians have long praised the 1570s maps of Flemish engraver Pieter Vanmolen for their careful craftsmanship. But a recent comparison with satellite imagery suggests that the maps lacked ______. On them, coastlines are misplaced by as much as 40 kilometers, and several rivers run through the wrong valleys.
explanation: Start with the evidence: the coastlines and rivers are badly misplaced. The word "lacked" reverses the blank, so the blank names the quality the maps did not have. Maps with errors of 40 kilometers lacked precision.

A.why: You matched the blank to the evidence (the maps are full of errors) and skipped the reversal. "Lacked distortion" would mean the maps were accurate, which is the exact opposite of what the satellite comparison found.

B.why: Ornament has nothing to do with misplaced coastlines and rivers. The evidence after the blank is about accuracy, not how the maps look.

D.why: The passage says nothing about how widely the maps were distributed. Misplaced rivers are evidence that the maps were inaccurate, not that few people saw them.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Woodblock prints are made by pressing paper against a single inked block, so art historians once assumed that impressions pulled from the same block would be virtually identical. However, when conservator Hana Ostrowski examined 40 surviving impressions of a 1790s landscape print, she found striking differences in ink density and line width from sheet to sheet. Her findings make it unlikely that the block's output was ever truly ______.
explanation: The evidence shows that the impressions differ noticeably. "Unlikely … ever truly" reverses the blank, so the blank has to be the opposite of differing. "Uniform" fits, and it echoes the older assumption that the prints were "virtually identical," which Ostrowski's findings undercut.

A.why: You matched the blank to the evidence (the sheets differ) and skipped the "unlikely" reversal. Saying it is unlikely the output was ever inconsistent would mean the prints matched, which is the opposite of what Ostrowski found.

B.why: Whether collectors wanted the prints never comes up. The findings are about how similar the impressions are, not about their market appeal.

C.why: Differences in ink density and line width say nothing about how many colors the print used. You would need evidence the passage doesn't give to rule out a single-color print.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Some climate researchers have predicted that rising winter temperatures will make heavy snowfall less ______ around North America's Great Lakes. Yet warmer lakes stay unfrozen later into the season and release more moisture into the cold air that passes over them. Weather records from Buffalo, New York, show that major lake-effect snowstorms have struck more often since 1950, not less.
explanation: The blank sits inside a prediction that the passage then knocks down with "Yet." The Buffalo records show snowstorms becoming more frequent, so the prediction being challenged must say snowfall would become less frequent. "Less common" says that, and the evidence that storms have "struck more often" contradicts it.

A.why: You matched the blank to what the evidence shows (more storms) and forgot the "less" in front of it. "Less rare" means more frequent, which would make the prediction agree with the Buffalo data instead of being contradicted by it.

B.why: Snow already falls only in certain seasons, and the evidence after "Yet" is about how often storms strike, not when in the year they arrive. "Less seasonal" doesn't set up the contrast the passage draws.

C.why: The passage gives no evidence about forecasting. A rise in how often storms strike doesn't refute a claim about predictability, so "Yet" would have nothing to push against.
